### INITIATION AND MODULATION OF ASTHMA PHARMACOTHERAPY

**Flowchart:**

* `Infrequent & Intermittent symptoms` $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ [Previous step/Maintenance]
* `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Levosalbutamol (50ug) OR Salbutamol (100 ug). 2 puffs sos`
* `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (<2 per week but >2 per month)`
* `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Refer`
    * (Poor Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Regular Symptoms (>2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year`
* `Refer`
    * (Good Control, $\downarrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
* `Add low dose oral corticosteroids`
    * (Good Control, $\uparrow$ arrow) $\rightarrow$ `Add tiotropium (9µg) 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine`

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

---

---

**TABLE 1. DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN ASTHMA AND CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE AIRWAY DISEASE (COPD)**

| | Asthma | COPD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Age of Onset** | More often in childhood or early adulthood; variable | Usually later in life (4th or 5th decade) |
| **Course** | Episodic | Progressive |
| **Smoking, other exposures** | Uncommon | Common |
| **Nasal Symptoms, Atopy** | Common | Rare |
| **Family History** | Often | Uncommon |
| **Triggers** | Often Identified | None |
| **Wheeze** | Prominent and almost universal | May or may not be present |

---

**TABLE 2. LEVEL OF CURRENT ASTHMA CONTROL (OVER THE PRECEDING FOUR WEEKS)**

| Components | Inadequately controlled (any one) | Adequately controlled (all should be present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication | More than twice a week | Twice or less in a week |
| Night-time symptoms/ awakening | Any | None |
| Limitation of activities | Any | None |
| Pulmonary function (if available) | FEV1 <80% of predicted or PEF <80% of personal best | FEV1 >80% of predicted or PEF >80% of personal best |

FEV1 Forced Expiratory Volume in first second, PEF Peak Expiratory Flow

# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

**AVOIDANCE OF PROVOKING AGENTS, MOISTURIZERS AND EARLY TREATMENT ARE THE AIM OF ECZEMA MANAGEMENT**

draft.title: Routine Care Plan: Occupational Contact Dermatitis

activities.description: Monitor the affected skin area for signs of secondary bacterial infection, including increased pain, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, or yellow crusting. Advise patient to seek prompt medical attention if these signs develop.

Strictly avoid further exposure to nickel. This includes avoiding the new bracelet and other potential sources such as costume jewelry, belt buckles, watch backs, and metal fasteners on clothing. Consider using barrier methods (e.g., clear nail polish on metal items) if avoidance is not fully possible, though removal is preferred.

Implement gentle skin care routine: Use mild, fragrance-free soap for bathing and apply moisturizers immediately after bathing while skin is damp. Apply moisturizers multiple times daily to maintain skin barrier integrity and reduce pruritus.
Advise keeping fingernails short and avoiding scratching to prevent skin breakdown and secondary infection. Use cool compresses for symptomatic relief of itching if needed.

Clinician to review current medication history. Patient reports no current medicines. Confirm absence of topical or oral medications previously used for dermatitis. Discuss appropriate topical therapy options (e.g., topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors) for active inflammation and pruritus control, considering lesion location and severity.
Refer to General Practitioner for routine management of the dermatitis, prescription of appropriate topical therapies if needed, and further patient education on allergen avoidance.

Schedule a routine follow-up appointment with the General Practitioner to assess response to treatment and ensure resolution of the dermatitis. If symptoms persist or worsen despite avoidance and initial care, consider referral to dermatology for patch testing to confirm nickel allergy and identify other potential allergens.
activities.timing: Within 2-4 weeks or as clinically indicated

# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

Follow up with the general practitioner to review response to treatment and adjust management plan as needed.

activities.description: Clarify the specific name, formulation, and dosage of the existing prescribed skin treatment to ensure appropriate usage and monitor for efficacy.
Advise on strict avoidance of the identified trigger (laundry soap) and proper hand hygiene to prevent further irritation. Use mild, fragrance-free cleansers and lukewarm water.

Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection, including increased pain, pus discharge, yellow crusting, or spreading erythema, which would require urgent reassessment.
Monitor for systemic symptoms such as fever or swelling of the face/throat, which would indicate a more severe reaction requiring immediate evaluation.
Conduct a generic clinician medication review to assess the efficacy and tolerability of the current prescribed skin treatment once the specific agent is identified.
Schedule a primary-care telephone review to discuss persistent symptoms, confirm the medication regimen, and obtain a written care plan.
Refer to a general practitioner for ongoing management if symptoms persist despite trigger avoidance and current treatment, or if specialist dermatology referral is not feasible.

# TREATMENT

### GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Avoidance of allergens and irritant materials
• Daily bath with mild soap, keep nails short, avoid scratching
• Moisturizer are cornerstone in the management of eczema; to be applied immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp and apply multiple times during the day
• Antihistamines for (eg. levocetirizine) for control of pruritus
• Topical corticosteroids (TCS) mild – Over face/ flexures genitals. Mid potent TCS over palms, soles and lichenified lesions
• Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs)- Face/ flexures genitals and/or as maintenance treatment
• If secondary infection (pain, pus discharge, yellow crust)- Treat with topical/ oral antibiotic as needed

### SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT
**Primary/Secondary Level**
• Treatment of active eczema: Daily use of TCS of appropriate strength until completely clear ± antihistamine (for sedative/antipruritic effects) ± oral antibiotic course (if superinfection) - (refer to STW on rational use of topical therapy)
• Maintenance treatment for area where lesions are more resistant to treatment or there is propensity for relapse, like flexural skin- Intermittent use of mid-potency TCS (e.g. 2-3 days/week) and/or TCI (e.g. 3–5 days/week)

**Tertiary Level**
• Severe disease in addition to above may require phototherapy or systemic treatment (Short course of oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine etc.)

***

**AVOIDANCE OF PROVOKING AGENTS, MOISTURIZERS AND EARLY TREATMENT ARE THE AIM OF ECZEMA MANAGEMENT**

scenario: Dermatitis and limited access to skin clinic

activities.description: Monitor for the development of red-flag symptoms, including new or worsening leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, unexplained weight loss, fever, or pain that is severe at night or unrelieved by rest. Encourage gentle movement and walking as tolerated. Reassure the patient that walking and normal daily activities are safe and beneficial for recovery, addressing concerns that movement may damage the back. Avoid prolonged bed rest.

Advise on activity modification, such as avoiding heavy lifting or twisting motions that exacerbate pain, while maintaining general mobility. Consider ergonomic adjustments for work or daily tasks if applicable.

Review current use of over-the-counter pain relief or other medications. Confirm that the patient has no known allergies and is not taking any prescription medications. Discuss appropriate use of OTC analgesics if needed, ensuring no contraindications exist.
activities.timing: At follow-up or if symptoms worsen

activities.description: Schedule routine follow-up in 2 to 6 weeks if symptoms do not continue to improve. Earlier review may be warranted if pain persists, worsens, or significantly impacts daily function.
Clarify the patient's specific concerns about walking and back damage to tailor education and reassurance strategies. Assess for any psychosocial factors contributing to kinesiophobia.
Confirm whether the patient has access to resources for gentle stretching or physical therapy exercises, which may aid recovery and reduce fear of movement.

Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of HEADACHE ICD-10-G43-44

**TREATMENT FLOWCHART**
**LEGEND/ INDEX/ KEY**
* Type of Headache (Green)
* Management at PHC (Yellow)
* Management at district hospital (Dark teal)

**Flowchart Pathways:**
* CONTINUOUS HEADACHES (Progressive headache of acute or subacute onset persisting more than 1 week. Possibilities: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis, Intra Cranial Space Occupying Lesion, Meningitis, Brain abscess) -> Referred to higher centre -> [CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram, Lumbar puncture, Refer to tertiary care centre]
* CHRONIC TENSION HEADACHE (Continuous bilateral headache for many years with significant insomnia and psychosomatic complaints.) -> Start Amitriptyline (10mg HS) and advice on lifestyle -> Brain imaging if atypical features exist
* MIGRAINE (Side alternating, associated visual aura, photo-phono phobia, nausea, relieved by sleep or analgesics) -> [Frequency > 2 /month - Start prophylaxis trial for 2 months: Propranolol 40 mg OD, Flunarizine 10 mg OD; Acute management: Analgesics (Paracetamol 650 mg, or Indomethacin 50 mg) and Antiemetics (Prochlorperazine 10mg). Lifestyle changes: Good sleep at least 6 hrs, food habit modification, avoiding triggers of migraine.] -> Brain imaging if there are atypical symptoms
* ATYPICAL MIGRAINE (Hemiplegia, visual impairment, vertigo) -> Analgesics for pain, Refer to higher centre with imaging facility -> [CT/ MRI with MR angiogram or CT angiogram if required, Migraine prophylaxis after ruling out stroke and other diseases]
* TRIGEMINAL AUTONOMIC CEPHALGIAS (Rapid onset peri orbital and temporal pain with autonomic features) -> Indomethacin (25mg TID) for 7 days -> Refer to tertiary care centre
* CLUSTER HEADACHE, PAROXYSMAL HEMICRANIAS, SHORT LASTING UNILATERAL NEURALGIFORM PAIN WITH CONJUNCTIVAL INJECTION AND TEARING SYNDROME (SUNCT) -> Refer to tertiary care centre -> Refer to tertiary care centre

**RED FLAG SIGNS**
* First or worst headache of the patient's life
* Focal neurologic signs (not typical aura)
* Severe headache awakening from sleep
* Headache with fever, change in personality, mental status, level of consciousness
* Fever, neck stiffness or meningism
* New onset of severe headache in pregnancy or postpartum or while on hormone treatment
* Rapid onset with strenuous exercise
* Sudden onset (maximal intensity occurs within seconds to minutes, thunderclap headache)
* New headache type in a patient with malignancy or immunosuppression

**REASONS FOR REFERRAL**
* Non responding headaches
* Headaches with danger signs should be immediately referred and investigated for potentially dangerous conditions

**TREATMENT OF MAJOR CATASTROPHIC HEADACHES AT TERTIARY CENTRE**
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE -> Angiogram, clipping/ coiling of aneurysm (to prevent rebleed)
* Sudden Severe headache, First or Worst headache of life -> CT with CT Angiogram/ MRI with MR angiogram -> INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE -> Stroke unit admission and neurosurgery for cortical hemorrhages or large hemorrhage with herniation
* Progressive headache -> MR venogram -> CEREBRAL VENOUS THROMBOSIS -> Intravenous UFH / subcutaneous heparin/LMWH
* Headache with fever, personality change, altered sensorium, neck stiffness -> CT scan followed by CSF study -> MENINGIOENCEPHALITIS -> Antibiotics/ antivirals
* Progressive headache with seizure or focal deficit -> CT/MRI with contrast -> BRAIN TUMORS -> Surgery, radiation, chemotherapy

**INDICATIONS FOR ADMISSION**
* Patient with unrelenting headache
* Immunosuppressed patients with continuous headache,
* First ever headache with worsening intensity,
* Progressive headache with other systemic disease
* Severe symptomatic primary headache disorders

**CRITERIA FOR DISCHARGE**
* Primary headache disorders- symptomatically improved severe episode of headache due to primary headache disorder can be discharged
* Secondary headache disorders- secondary headache disorders with essential work up, diagnosis and treatment as per individual case can be discharged

**FOLLOW UP OF HEADACHE PATIENTS**
| CAUSES OF HEADACHE | TREATMENT OF HEADACHE |
| :--- | :--- |
| Intra cerebral hemorrhage | Good control of blood pressure |
| Seizures | Antiepileptic medications |
| Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis | Follow up of anticoagulation |
| Migraine | Give prophylaxis for adequate duration of time and taper after remission |

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

Clinician to review current non-pharmacological management efficacy. Discuss appropriate use of over-the-counter analgesics if needed, ensuring avoidance of medication-overuse headache by limiting frequency of use.

scenario: Tension headache with disrupted shift sleep

activities.description: Ascertain the specific dose and frequency of paracetamol usage to evaluate for medication overuse headache (MOH) risk, given use on most headache days.

Implement lifestyle modifications including maintaining regular sleep patterns (at least 6-8 hours), managing stress, staying hydrated, and identifying/avoiding individual headache triggers.
Conduct a comprehensive medication review to assess total analgesic consumption days per month, evaluate for medication overuse headache, and review appropriateness of current paracetamol regimen.
Schedule a routine appointment with the general practitioner to review the headache diary, clarify paracetamol dosing, and finalize the written care plan.

activities.description: Monitor for resolution of sore throat and associated symptoms. Advise patient to seek urgent care if symptoms worsen or if red flags develop, including difficulty breathing, drooling, inability to swallow fluids, high-grade fever, or severe neck pain/stiffness.
Encourage adequate rest and hydration. Suggest symptomatic relief measures such as warm saltwater gargles, warm liquids, and throat lozenges to alleviate discomfort.

Review current medication history. Patient reports no current medicines. Confirm absence of regular medications and discuss appropriate use of over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., paracetamol or ibuprofen) for pain and fever if required, ensuring no contraindications.
activities.timing: At follow-up or if symptoms persist

activities.description: Clarify allergy status. Current record states 'Allergy status not documented'. Confirm any known drug or food allergies to ensure safety of any future or over-the-counter medication use.

Schedule routine follow-up if symptoms do not improve within 3-5 days or if they persist beyond 7-10 days. Re-evaluate for potential bacterial etiology (e.g., Group A Streptococcus) if symptoms worsen or fail to resolve, considering Centor criteria assessment.

If symptoms persist or worsen, consider throat swab for culture or rapid antigen detection test (RADT) to rule out bacterial pharyngitis, particularly if Centor criteria suggest higher likelihood of Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus.
activities.timing: Conditional on symptom persistence or worsening

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
* Icon of head with nose/eyes -> Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a **viral etiology**. Pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
* Icon of head/throat profile -> Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest Epiglottitis or Laryngotracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients
* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

## MANAGEMENT | PHC / PRIMARY LEVEL | DISTRICT HOSPITAL | | :--- | :--- | | 1. Assess the patient for signs of toxicity, epiglottitis or oropharyngeal abscess

3. Saltwater gargle, warm liquids, and rest may be helpful in relieving symptoms

5. Antibiotic therapy:
   a. Patients positive for all 4 Centor criteria to be treated with antibiotics without waiting for antigen testing or cultures

• Deep neck space infection
• Diphtheria
• Epiglottitis

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
* Icon of head with nose/eyes -> Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a **viral etiology**. Pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
* Icon of head/throat profile -> Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest Epiglottitis or Laryngotracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients
* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

## MANAGEMENT | PHC / PRIMARY LEVEL | DISTRICT HOSPITAL | | :--- | :--- | | 1. Assess the patient for signs of toxicity, epiglottitis or oropharyngeal abscess
2. Ensure vitals/ hydration of the patient
3. Saltwater gargle, warm liquids, and rest may be helpful in relieving symptoms
4. Ibuprofen or Paracetamol is recommended for analgesia
5. Antibiotic therapy:
   a. Patients positive for all 4 Centor criteria to be treated with antibiotics without waiting for antigen testing or cultures
   b. Patients with Centor score of 2&3 to be treated with antibiotics only if antigen testing or throat swab culture is positive
   c. Patients with Centor score of only 1 not to be treated with antibiotics
   d. Amoxicillin (50 mg/kg/d in 2-3 doses orally) for 10 days is the first choice for GABHS infection. For patients who are sensitive for penicillin group, Erythromycin or Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice
6. Parenteral antibiotics (Ceftriaxone/ cefotaxime) and steroids are to be started when the airway is compromised due to suspected epiglottis/ Croup. | Management of complication e.g.
• Deep neck space infection
• Diphtheria
• Epiglottitis
• Croup | ---

## INVESTIGATIONS

| ESSENTIAL | OPTIONAL | DESIRABLE |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Throat swab for culture, routine hemogram including total and differential leukocyte counts and peripheral smear to look for atypical lymphocytes (seen in IM). | GABHS rapid antigen detection test (RADT) | Lab tests to rule out EB Virus, Coxsackie virus, Herpes virus, fungal or Gonococcal pharyngitis |

## FOLLOW UP SERVICES

Recurrent (more than 7 episodes in previuos year or 5/year in last two years or 3/year in last 3 years) tonsillitis episodes need to be evaluated for tonsillectomy.

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

---

**ABBREVIATIONS**
**GABHS:** Group A Beta Hemolyticus Streptococcus
**GERD:** Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease
**LRTI:** Lower Respiratory Tract Infection
**EB:** Epstein Barr
**RADT:** Rapid Antigen Detection Test

draft.title: Routine Care Plan: Viral Pharyngitis

scenario: Early sore throat with normal intake

activities.description: Monitor for red flag symptoms including worsening throat pain, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), drooling, breathing difficulty, high-grade fever, or unilateral tonsillar swelling, which may suggest complications such as peritonsillar abscess or epiglottitis.
Continue supportive care with adequate hydration, rest, and warm fluids. Saltwater gargles may provide symptomatic relief for throat discomfort.

Attend the scheduled routine clinic reassessment tomorrow for clinical evaluation of persistent symptoms, including oropharyngeal examination and assessment of Centor criteria if bacterial etiology is suspected.
Consider throat swab for culture or rapid antigen detection test (RADT) if clinical examination suggests bacterial pharyngitis (e.g., high Centor score) to guide further management.

Review current medication use and allergies. Although no current medicines are reported, verify absence of over-the-counter analgesic use and confirm allergy status to ensure safe management if pharmacological intervention is considered.
Clarify allergy status, as it is currently undocumented. Confirm any known drug allergies, particularly to penicillins or macrolides, to inform potential future treatment decisions.
Clarify if the patient has experienced recurrent episodes of tonsillitis or pharyngitis in the past, as this may influence long-term management considerations.

activities.description: Implement environmental controls to reduce throat irritation. Utilize the available colleague to swap locations away from the smoking area at the tea stall for several days, as requested by the patient.

activities.description: Continue symptomatic self-care including adequate fluid intake, rest, and use of over-the-counter symptom relief measures (e.g., throat lozenges, warm liquids) as needed for comfort.
Monitor for resolution of symptoms, which typically occur within 7 to 10 days for viral upper respiratory infections. Watch for any worsening of throat pain, fever, or development of new symptoms.

Monitor for red flags indicating complications or alternative diagnoses, such as breathing difficulty, drooling, high-grade fever, unilateral tonsillar enlargement, or inability to maintain hydration.
Re-evaluate if symptoms persist beyond 10 days, worsen significantly, or if red flags develop. Consider reassessment for bacterial etiology or other complications if clinical picture changes.

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
* Icon of head with nose/eyes -> Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a **viral etiology**. Pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
* Icon of head/throat profile -> Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest Epiglottitis or Laryngotracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients
* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

---

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

• Epiglottitis

activities.description: Interview assessment recommendation: Seek urgent care now. Assessment actions: Arrange urgent in-person clinical assessment today. Longer-term activities must not replace or delay this recommendation.

Monitor for signs of worsening dehydration (e.g., dizziness, confusion, very dark urine, inability to keep down even small sips) and airway compromise (e.g., drooling, stridor, difficulty breathing, muffled 'hot potato' voice).
activities.timing: Immediate and ongoing until urgent assessment

activities.description: Track fluid intake and urine output frequency/color. Note any fever development or worsening pain that prevents oral intake.
Urgent clinical assessment to evaluate hydration status (vitals, mucous membranes, skin turgor) and oropharyngeal exam to rule out complications such as peritonsillar abscess or epiglottitis.

Consider throat swab for culture or rapid antigen detection test (RADT) if bacterial etiology (e.g., Group A Strep) is suspected based on clinical criteria (Centor score), despite initial viral diagnosis.
Encourage small, frequent sips of clear fluids (water, oral rehydration solutions) to maintain hydration. Use warm liquids or saltwater gargles for symptomatic relief if tolerated.

Clinician to review current medication history (reported as none) and assess need for analgesia/antipyretics (e.g., paracetamol or ibuprofen) for pain and fever management, considering hydration status and renal function.
Confirm allergy status, as it is currently undocumented. Verify if there are any known drug allergies before prescribing any new medications.
Arrange follow-up if symptoms persist beyond typical viral course (7-10 days) or if complications arise. Re-evaluate hydration status after urgent intervention.
activities.timing: Conditional on outcome of urgent assessment

2. Ensure vitals/ hydration of the patient
3. Saltwater gargle, warm liquids, and rest may be helpful in relieving symptoms
4. Ibuprofen or Paracetamol is recommended for analgesia
5. Antibiotic therapy:
   a. Patients positive for all 4 Centor criteria to be treated with antibiotics without waiting for antigen testing or cultures
   b. Patients with Centor score of 2&3 to be treated with antibiotics only if antigen testing or throat swab culture is positive
   c. Patients with Centor score of only 1 not to be treated with antibiotics
   d. Amoxicillin (50 mg/kg/d in 2-3 doses orally) for 10 days is the first choice for GABHS infection. For patients who are sensitive for penicillin group, Erythromycin or Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice
6. Parenteral antibiotics (Ceftriaxone/ cefotaxime) and steroids are to be started when the airway is compromised due to suspected epiglottis/ Croup. | Management of complication e.g.
• Deep neck space infection

# Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of PHARYNGITIS AND SORE THROAT
### ICD-10-J02

**CLINICAL SCENARIOS**
Acute pharyngitis may include a spectrum of disease varying from simple viral pharyngitis to dreaded neck space infection.

**Clinical Scenario Timeline:**
* Icon of doctor and patient -> Acute onset of throat pain with or without – Fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in **bacterial pharyngitis**. Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
* Icon of head with nose/eyes -> Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a **viral etiology**. Pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
* Icon of head/throat profile -> Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest Epiglottitis or Laryngotracheobronchitis, especially in pediatric patients
* Icon of throat/tonsils -> An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests **Diphtheria**
* Icon of lymph node -> Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with **Infectious Mononucleosis(IM)**
* Icon of cigarette and reflux -> Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

## CLINICAL EXAMINATION

**PRELIMINARY**
* Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
* Check for vitals/ signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake due to odynophagia
* Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
* Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
* Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
* Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in IM
* A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with IM empirically treated with penicillin

**DESIRABLE**
Assess Centor criteria and ascertain its score

**RED FLAGS**
* Generalized lymphadenopathy
* Cardiac murmurs
* Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of LRTI
* Hot potato voice
* Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
* Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
* Agranulocyosis
* Epidemic of flu

**CENTOR SCORE TABLE**

| CLINICAL FEATURES | CENTOR SCORE | UNLIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | LIKELY TO HAVE GABHS | REQUIRE LAB TESTS TO CONFIRM GABHS INFECTION |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Fever | 1 | Score = 0-1 | Score = 4 | Score = 2-3 |
| Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | 1 | | | |
| Tonsillar exudate | 1 | | | |
| Absence of cough | 1 | | | |

## FOLLOW UP SERVICES

Recurrent (more than 7 episodes in previuos year or 5/year in last two years or 3/year in last 3 years) tonsillitis episodes need to be evaluated for tonsillectomy.

**KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES**

---

**GABHS:** Group A Beta Hemolyticus Streptococcus
**GERD:** Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease
**LRTI:** Lower Respiratory Tract Infection
**EB:** Epstein Barr
**RADT:** Rapid Antigen Detection Test
